analysis.title: Behind The Chip Curve: Goldman Admits AI Blew Up Its Inflation Forecast As Fed Hawks Circle
key_insights: Goldman expected core PCE at 2.3% by August in January. August core PCE came in at 3.0%, a 0.7pp overshoot.

Goldman's post-mortem (economist Abhay Duggirala, US Daily 'Where Has Inflation Surprised?') attributes more than 0.3pp of the overshoot to consumer electronics, reflecting a larger-than-expected AI-related boost to consumer prices.

Computer software and accessories alone account for 0.2pp of the surprise. Goldman estimates this component is overstated by 0.1pp because it gets too much weight in PCE (roughly 30 times the CPI weight) and is not quality-adjusted.

The article's own waterfall of the 0.7% overshoot: roughly 0.3% AI-exposed electronics, 0.3% energy passthrough from the Iran war, 0.1% each from tariffs and shelter, and -0.2% from pharma and used cars. This is the author's simplification of Goldman's Exhibit 1.

Goldman expects roughly three-fourths of the surprise (oil shock, tariffs, software/accessories) to fade over the next year as memory price pressures ease. About 0.2pp is genuine upside, mostly from housing and other AI-exposed electronics. Goldman forecasts core PCE falling to 2.2% by December 2027.

BEA changed the methodology on software and accessories last month. BofA calculates that revisions to software, portfolio management and legal services knocked 35bps off July core PCE, yet core PCE is still 3.0%.

September FOMC minutes: all 19 officials backed September's hike to 3.75%-4.00%, and most participants see another hike by year end. Staff attributed elevated inflation partly to technology-related consumer goods prices tied to the AI buildout.

Some participants said the AI buildout could push aggregate demand above aggregate supply over the medium term. A couple said a higher policy rate would help keep sector-specific price increases from energy disruptions and AI demand from broadening out.

BofA (Stephen Juneau, US Economic Weekly) says the FOMC is nearly unanimous that inflation risks are skewed to the upside, with the Fed's diffusion index of core PCE risk weightings near the top of its post-2021 range.

SF Fed's Mary Daly sees AI-driven chip and tech price pressure 'less as a one-off' and says relief is probably further out. She notes some companies are seeking forward contracts for memory chips and others are re-engineering products to use fewer chips.

Rabobank (Molly Schwartz) says Warsh's proposal to incorporate AI's deflationary effects into Fed forecasts appears delayed. It expects one more hike at the December FOMC, then a hold through 2027. Computer software and accessories prices have risen since the start of 2026, bucking the deflationary trend for the first time since 1998.

Chicago Fed's Goolsbee warned that the expectation of an AI productivity boom could itself overheat the economy over the next six months. KC Fed's Schmid said the Fed is fighting to control inflation and maintain credibility.

St. Louis Fed's Musalem told Reuters that more policy firming will be required and rates ought to be going up in the next 6 to 9 months. The NY Fed survey showed one-year inflation expectations at 3.9%, the highest since May 2023.

The Bank of Japan's regional report says raw-material-driven price increases are spreading to consumer goods. Markets read it as cementing another BoJ hike this year, which is a risk for US yields via Japanese repatriation.

Temasek CIO Rohit Sipahimalani named AI and inflation as the two key risks for 2027, saying an unwinding of the AI trade is the biggest risk but not imminent. Temasek plans to shift AI exposure from about half in public markets to 70%-75%.

Hyperscalers are not interest-rate sensitive, so fed funds hikes do little to slow AI demand for memory and chips. BofA projects hyperscaler capex up roughly 90% y/y this year and 36% next year. JPMorgan's Market Intel desk puts it at $805B in 2026 and $1.1T in 2027.

BNP Paribas expects AI-related memory markets to stay undersupplied through 2028, with 2026 pricing nearly tripling and non-AI demand bearing the cost. SK Group's chairman warned the crunch may last until 2030.

BofA's counterpoint: the direct inflationary impact is likely to remain limited absent meaningful supply constraints like 2020-23, because electrical equipment, computers and electronics are a small share of consumption. BofA also flags faster wage growth in data-center-linked industries.

Market event: last week the Nasdaq fell after the FT reported OpenAI's annualized revenue is about $20B below what had been signaled, hitting chipmakers and Oracle. The move reversed the next day and stocks returned to an all-time high.

risk_factors: Core goods inflation from AI-driven electronics and memory prices broadens out, as the BoJ is already seeing in Japan.
The Fed ends up behind the curve, hiking into an economy where the sector driving prices is insensitive to borrowing costs.
Memory supply constraints persist to 2028-2030, and Chinese CXMT supply may be blocked.
Faster wage growth in data-center-linked industries creates second-round inflation effects (BofA).
An unwinding of the AI trade, which Temasek calls the biggest 2027 risk.
Further BoJ hikes and Japanese repatriation pressure US Treasury yields.
charts_described: Goldman Exhibit 1 breaks down the August core PCE surprise by component. The top is dominated by software and accessories (~0.24pp) and other electronics (~0.1pp), air transport is second, and pharma is the largest offset.
BofA chart shows the Fed's diffusion index of core PCE risk weightings near the top of its post-2021 range.
vol_and_positioning: Last week the Nasdaq tumbled after the FT report on OpenAI revenue, then recovered the next day to an all-time high.
Temasek is shifting AI exposure from roughly half public markets to 70%-75% so it can pivot quickly.
geopolitical: War with Iran is passing through to energy prices, including jet fuel and air transport, and added roughly 0.3% to the core PCE overshoot per the article's waterfall.
Tariffs continue to add to core goods inflation, though the FOMC minutes say tariff effects are waning while AI buildout effects increase.
Washington may block Chinese memory production (CXMT), which Acer's CEO said would ease memory prices in 2027.
Japanese repatriation flows have been pressuring Treasuries, and a further BoJ hike is expected this year.

tension_points.bull_case: Goldman and BofA argue the inflation surprise is largely one-time or mismeasurement. About three-fourths should fade as memory pressure eases, with core PCE falling to 2.2% by December 2027. BofA says the direct impact is limited because electronics are a small share of consumption.
tension_points.bear_case: The Fed minutes and Daly see AI price pressure as less of a one-off. Memory is undersupplied through 2028 (BNP) or 2030 (SK Group), hyperscalers ignore rates, and wage growth in data-center industries is faster, which raises the risk of broadening.
tension_points.what_invalidates: BofA's caveat: the benign view holds only absent meaningful supply constraints akin to 2020-23. Persistent memory shortages would break it.

tension_points.bull_case: Fed's Lisa Cook and Warsh argue short-term adoption costs will be priced out and long-term productivity gains could drive disinflation within a few years.
tension_points.bear_case: Goolsbee warns the expectation of an AI productivity boom could overheat the economy in the next six months. Rabobank says AI is inflationary for now.
